modules.title: The Forward-Deployed Career
modules.summary: Welcome to IL-10, Portfolio, Career & Professional Practice — the career academy of the Interstitium Labs university. I'm your instructor for this course, and my job here is different from the technical tracks: the proof of work is already in your portfolio — this course turns it into a career you run deliberately. This is Module 1: The Forward-Deployed Career. Over this module we're going to run the six-move FDE arc — discover, model, prove, integrate, operate, generalize — and build the outcome layer on top of it: AI-matched applications tracked against skills you've actually earned, a conversion funnel that diagnoses its own bottlenecks, and interview systems for technical depth, system design, behavioral stories, and offers. By the end you'll have a career operating system, not a stack of good intentions.
objectives: Discover: find the customer's real problem beneath the stated one.
Model and prove: build the technical case with evidence.
Integrate and operate: ship inside customer constraints; transfer operations.
Generalize: turn engagement learnings into product.
Run interviews: technical, design, behavioral, offers.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The vocabulary of the forward-deployed career — every term below is a working tool, not decoration:
- **Forward-deployed engineer (FDE)** — an engineer who ships inside the customer's environment: their compliance, their change windows, their team operating the result after handoff.
- **Discover** — the first arc move: finding the customer's real problem beneath the stated one. Diagnose like a doctor — symptoms → tests → diagnosis.
- **Model** — the second arc move: building a technical representation of the problem and the candidate solution.
- **Prove** — the third arc move: the technical core. Prototype the risky parts first and prove with data, using the smallest decisive experiment.
- **Integrate** — the fourth arc move: shipping inside the customer — their compliance, their change windows, their constraints.
- **Operate** — the fifth arc move: running the solution inside the customer and transferring operations to their team.
- **Generalize** — the sixth arc move: turning learnings from engagements into reusable product. The pattern across three engagements is the signal — not every engagement becomes product.
- **AI-matched applications** — matching your proven skills to role requirements: apply where the evidence fits, not where the title flatters.
- **Application tracking against skills earned** — every application cites portfolio proof; the catalog's nodes become resume bullets with proof links.
- **The funnel** — applied → response → screen → onsite → offer. Conversion at each stage diagnoses the bottleneck: low response → fix the resume/portfolio; low conversion → fix the interview system; low offers → fix the close. The funnel is the strategy document.
- **System design interview** — a conversation, not a monologue: requirements → estimates → API → data model → scale → trade-offs, practiced aloud, clarifying questions first.
- **Behavioral interview (the FDE story)** — STAR with forward-deployed flavor: the customer constraint, your diagnosis, the shipped outcome, the transfer — with numbers.
- **Offer evaluation** — total comp, growth, team, and the walk-away number — decided BEFORE the offer arrives.
- **Walk-away number** — a pre-committed compensation floor. Prevents the worst negotiation mistake: accepting from desperation.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run one complete FDE cycle on a real problem — even a small one. This is the procedure, in order:
1. **Pick the problem.** A friend's business, an open-source issue, a process at a part-time job — small is fine, real is mandatory.
2. **Discover.** Ask the key question first: 'what happens if we do nothing?' The problem's value lives in the answer. Write down the stated problem, then the diagnosed problem — they will differ.
3. **Model and prove.** Name the riskiest assumption. Design the smallest decisive experiment that could kill it. Run it within weeks, not quarters — the FDE doesn't have quarters, they have weeks. Document the evidence.
4. **Integrate and operate.** List the 'customer' constraints (compliance, change windows, who maintains it). Ship inside them. Write the transfer doc so their team can operate it after you — the transfer is the deliverable.
5. **Generalize review.** Ask: which learnings compound into something reusable? File the pattern. Not every engagement becomes product; the pattern across three does.
6. **Run the outcome layer.** Match your proven skills to five real roles (evidence, not titles). Apply with portfolio citations. Log every stage in the funnel tracker (see the course script lab), compute conversion at each stage, and fix ONLY the bottleneck stage.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
**Capstone: the FDE engagement dossier.** You are the forward-deployed engineer; deliver the dossier a client would pay for:
- A **discovery memo** (one page): the stated problem, your diagnosis, and the answer to 'what happens if we do nothing?'
- **Proof**: the smallest decisive experiment you ran, the evidence it produced, and what it killed or confirmed.
- A **funnel report**: 20+ real applications logged in the funnel tracker, conversion at each stage, and your bottleneck diagnosis with the single fix you're applying.
- **Three STAR stories** in FDE format — customer constraint, diagnosis, shipped outcome with numbers, transfer — rehearsed aloud until tight (the course's STAR Story Builder trainer is built for this).
- An **offer evaluation rubric**: total comp, growth, team — and your walk-away number, written down before any offer exists.
Done right, this dossier is portfolio artifact, interview prep, and career plan in one.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Everything in this module is practice material I authored for this course — the arc, the funnels, the story formats, the scenarios. Interstitium Labs confers no certificate, and nothing here is a credential, a job guarantee, or career advice about any specific employer. The interview frameworks describe how to prepare and perform; they don't certify outcomes. Track your real results in the funnel — the data is the honest part.

modules.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
modules.summary: Welcome back — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Self-Knowledge. You can't direct a career you haven't examined, so before we build ventures or climb ladders, we're going to take the Jung-typology instrument — the Humanmetrics assessment — and treat it as exactly what it is: working-style data for career decisions. Not a box, not a destiny, not a hiring tool — data. You'll learn what the four dichotomies actually measure, how to map type to role-family fit as a hypothesis, how to compose teams from complementary styles, and how to write a development plan that grows your range instead of replacing who you are.
objectives: Take the typology instrument and interpret it as working-style data.
Map type to role-family fit — as hypothesis, not destiny.
Design team composition with complementary styles.
Write a development plan for the non-preferred functions.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The instrument and its honest interpretation — preferences as data:
- **Jung typology** — a preference instrument measuring stable preferences in how you process information and make decisions. It measures preferences; it does NOT measure ability, intelligence, character, or destiny.
- **Extraversion / Introversion (E/I)** — energy source: whether interaction or solitude recharges you. An introvert can present brilliantly; it just costs more energy.
- **Sensing / Intuition (S/N)** — information: concrete detail and the present versus patterns, possibilities, and the future.
- **Thinking / Feeling (T/F)** — decisions: impersonal logic and criteria versus values and human impact.
- **Judging / Perceiving (J/P)** — lifestyle: settled plans and closure versus open options and flexibility.
- **Working styles** — the 16 types read as styles of working, not boxes. Use for insight, not identity.
- **Career-fit mapping** — type-to-role-family hypotheses: e.g., INTJ/INTP patterns in architecture and research, ESFJ/ENFJ patterns in customer-facing leadership. Fit is energy economics: where does the work energize you versus drain you? Hypothesis, not destiny — no type is 'best' for tech; the industry needs all 16.
- **Working-style implications** — how you recharge, decide, and organize. Design your workday around the answers — and use it in interviews: 'I do my best deep work when...' is self-knowledge as a selling point.
- **Team composition** — complementary styles: the visionary needs the finisher; the analyst needs the diplomat.
- **Development plan** — deliberate practice of the non-preferred functions: the thinker practices naming stakeholder impact; the judger practices holding ambiguity; the introvert practices visible communication. Range, not replacement — one stretch behavior per quarter, small, observable, reviewable.
- **Retake variance** — normal. Treat borderline dichotomies as flexible and context-dependent, not fixed labels.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Turn the instrument into a working self-knowledge file. Steps:
1. **Take it honestly.** Use the Humanmetrics instrument linked in this course's source links. Answer as you are, not as the job posting wants.
2. **Record all four letters** and the strength of each preference. Flag every borderline — near-even splits are the honest answer, and they're flexible, not fixed.
3. **Write the working-style profile** (one page): how you recharge, how you decide, how you organize — then design your workday around the answers. Which hours get deep work? Which meetings drain you, and how do you recover?
4. **Map to role families as hypothesis.** List three role families you're considering. For each, score the energy economics: where would this work energize you, where would it drain you? Remember — hypothesis, not destiny.
5. **Compose a team.** Design a hypothetical four-person project team with complementary styles covering vision, analysis, finishing, and diplomacy. Name what each style contributes and what breaks if one is missing.
6. **Write the development plan.** Pick ONE non-preferred function. Define one observable stretch behavior for this quarter (e.g., 'name stakeholder impact explicitly in every proposal'). Review it quarterly. The plan lives with the career plan — self-knowledge directs the FDE arc.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
**Project: the self-knowledge dossier.** Deliver a four-part brief you can actually use:
- **(1) Your result**, with borderline dichotomies flagged and interpreted as flexible — no fixed labels.
- **(2) A one-page working-style profile** — 'I do my best deep work when...' — written in language you can use verbatim in interviews.
- **(3) A team-composition plan** for a hypothetical four-person project: the four styles, what each contributes, and the failure mode if the finisher (or the diplomat) is missing.
- **(4) A one-quarter development plan**: one non-preferred function, one observable stretch behavior, and the review date.
This dossier is a career artifact: it feeds your interview answers, your team choices, and your quarterly reviews.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: This module is self-knowledge practice, not psychology. The instrument is a preference questionnaire — useful for reflection, working-style insight, and career-fit hypotheses; it is not a medical device, not a measure of ability or worth, and never a tool for hiring decisions about other people. Treat your type as data about yourself, hold it lightly, and retake it if life changes you. Interstitium Labs confers no certificate.

modules.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3: Entrepreneurship — the Babson-informed track. I'm your instructor, and here's my promise for this module: we're going to treat entrepreneurship as a discipline with a literature — opportunity recognition, resource marshaling, risk management — not a mystical calling. You'll audit the Babson curriculum map against a venture's real needs, practice problem discovery (pains with budgets), run the MVP discipline as experiments instead of products, model unit economics until the spreadsheet tells you scale, fix, or kill, and learn fundraising literacy so you can read a SAFE before you ever sign one. The contemporary practitioner model — operators teaching operators — is our frame: borrow the proof-of-work, skip the credential worship.
objectives: Audit the Babson curriculum map against your venture's needs.
Discover problems worth solving: pains with budgets.
Practice the MVP discipline: smallest test of the riskiest assumption.
Model unit economics; speak fundraising literacy.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The venture vocabulary — each term is a decision tool:
- **Problem discovery** — finding pains with budgets: the problem must hurt AND have a payer. Fun without a budget is a hobby, not a venture.
- **MVP discipline** — the smallest test of the riskiest assumption. An experiment, not a product — concierge and Wizard-of-Oz tests count.
- **Unit economics** — the per-customer math: CAC, LTV, payback period, contribution margin. The bar: LTV:CAC ≥ 3 and payback < 12 months — or the model doesn't work.
- **CAC (customer acquisition cost)** — what you pay to win one customer.
- **LTV (lifetime value)** — the gross profit expected from one customer over the whole relationship: ARPU × margin ÷ churn.
- **Payback period** — CAC ÷ monthly gross profit per customer. Under 12 months is the bar.
- **Fundraising literacy** — SAFEs and convertibles, dilution, the pitch as a story with numbers. Raise from strength or don't raise — fundraising is a tactic, not the goal.
- **SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity)** — invest now, price later. Know the cap and the discount before you sign.
- **Default alive / default dead** — can you reach profitability on current cash? Alive = yes. Plan the path to default alive explicitly.
- **Curriculum audit** — mapping your venture's needs against the disciplines (finance, marketing, operations): hire or learn to cover the gaps. It prevents the classic failure — a strong product with no distribution.
- **Entrepreneurship as a discipline** — opportunity recognition, resource marshaling, risk management: teachable, not mystical. The three founder literacies are finance, marketing, and operations — read a P&L, acquire a customer, deliver the thing.
- **Practitioner-led education** — operators teaching operators: war stories over textbooks. Borrow: practitioner instructors, project-based proof, hiring-partner integration. Avoid: credential worship, debt for signaling, curriculum as content marketing.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Worked estimation: the unit-economics verdict, step by step. This is the exact calculation behind the course's unit-economics script lab — follow it by hand once, then automate it:
1. **Write down the inputs.** CAC = $120, ARPU = $25/month, gross margin = 0.8, monthly churn = 0.05.
2. **Compute LTV.** LTV = ARPU × margin ÷ churn = 25 × 0.8 ÷ 0.05 = $400.
3. **Compute the ratio.** LTV ÷ CAC = 400 ÷ 120 ≈ 3.3 — clears the ≥ 3 bar.
4. **Compute payback.** Payback = CAC ÷ (ARPU × margin) = 120 ÷ 20 = 6 months — under the 12-month bar.
5. **Read the verdict.** Ratio ≥ 3 and payback < 12 → SCALE: the economics work.
6. **Know the other branches.** Ratio ≥ 2 but a bar missed → FIX: improve retention or monetization before scale. Below that → KILL or rebuild: scaling a broken unit is just faster dying.
7. **Apply the sanity rule.** Unit economics before scale, unit economics before virality — the spreadsheet is the strategy.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
**Project: the venture brief.** You're the founder; deliver the brief an honest investor would respect:
- **(1) A problem statement** with a named payer and budget evidence — pains with budgets, not vibes.
- **(2) An MVP experiment design** for the riskiest assumption: the smallest decisive test (concierge and Wizard-of-Oz welcome), what kills the idea, what confirms it.
- **(3) A unit-economics model**: your CAC, LTV, payback, and contribution margin, with the verdict rule applied — scale, fix, or kill, in writing. Run the course's unit-economics script lab on your numbers.
- **(4) A one-page fundraising-literacy memo**: SAFE terms (cap, discount), a dilution sketch, and your call — raise from strength, or run default-alive.
- **(5) A curriculum audit**: the three founder literacies against your venture's needs — what you'll learn, what you'll hire for.
Remember: the founder's curriculum is the venture itself.

Nothing here is investment, legal, or financial advice: SAFEs and dilution are real instruments, so get qualified counsel before signing anything, and confirm current program terms with the institutions themselves. Interstitium Labs confers no certificate and is not affiliated with Babson or Y Combinator.

modules.title: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 4: Quantitative Finance — the ladder. I'm your instructor, and I want to be straight with you up front: this module is a preparation map, not a shortcut. We're going to audit the prerequisites honestly (proof-level math, probability at depth, programming), map the internship timeline — the interviews start a year before the internship — work through the MIT MicroMasters in Finance as a graduate-level on-ramp with a real proctored comprehensive exam, and finish at the fork: desk quant, researcher, or consultant. Three different games. You'll choose with your eyes open, in writing.
objectives: Audit prerequisites: the math, probability, and programming the ladder demands.
Map internships: the on-ramps and their timelines.
Prepare the MicroMasters: graduate finance + the proctored comprehensive.
Choose the fork: desk quant, researcher, or consultant — eyes open.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The ladder's vocabulary — each term marks a rung or a gate:
- **Prerequisite audit** — the honest inventory: proof-level calculus, linear algebra, and probability; Python (pandas/numpy) and C++ for latency-sensitive work. Gaps compound — fix them before the ladder.
- **Probability at depth** — the interview core: the classic coins-and-dice problems, solved at depth and under time.
- **Stochastic calculus** — the mathematics of random processes; the language derivatives pricing is written in.
- **Itô's lemma** — the chain rule for stochastic processes: d(W²) = 2W dW + dt. The dt term is the whole point — it comes from the quadratic variation of Brownian motion, dW² = dt.
- **MIT MicroMasters in Finance** — graduate-level finance courses: asset pricing, derivatives, financial engineering. This module maps preparation for it; it does not grant it.
- **Proctored comprehensive exam** — the credential's teeth: identity-verified, rigorous. The filter — prepare like it matters, because it does.
- **Degree-pathway value** — credit toward the master's: the MicroMasters as an on-ramp, not just a certificate. Do the transfer math before enrolling.
- **Desk quant** — implements models close to P&L: implementation speed and correctness under pressure. Desk roles hire at bachelor's/master's with proof-level math and C++/Python.
- **Researcher** — novel mathematics, publication-adjacent work. Skews PhD.
- **Consultant** — breadth, clients, travel. The case interview is its own sport: structured problem-solving, mental math, framework first — practice cases, not just math.
- **The internship map** — the timelines: sophomore → junior summer, and the interviews start a year before the internship.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Worked estimation: Itô's lemma applied to W², step by step. This is the technical heart of the module — follow it by hand until the dt term feels inevitable:
1. **State the tool.** Itô's formula: for a smooth f and standard Brownian motion W, df = f′(W) dW + ½ f″(W) dt.
2. **Pick the function.** f(x) = x², so f′(x) = 2x and f″(x) = 2.
3. **Substitute.** d(W²) = 2W dW + ½·2·dt = 2W dW + dt.
4. **Read the result.** The ordinary chain rule would give only 2W dW. Stochastic calculus adds the drift correction dt — that term is the whole point, and it comes from dW² = dt, the quadratic variation of Brownian motion.
5. **Generalize once.** For f(x) = x³: f′ = 3x², f″ = 6x, so d(W³) = 3W² dW + 3W dt. Same machinery, every time.
6. **Connect it.** Graduate finance is applied stochastic calculus — this is why the math module wasn't optional.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
**Project: the quant-ladder plan.** Deliver a written plan with five parts:
- **(1) A prerequisite audit** with honest gap flags: calculus, linear algebra, and probability at proof level (not cookbook); Python and C++. Gaps get study blocks, not wishful thinking.
- **(2) A 12-week probability-depth schedule**: timed problem sets, coins-and-dice at depth, code interviews where you implement the math (stochastic simulation in an hour).
- **(3) An internship timeline** worked backward from your target summers — applications and interviews a year ahead.
- **(4) A MicroMasters preparation map**: which IL-02/IL-10 nodes prepare each graduate course, plus a transfer-math worksheet — credit terms verified with MIT before enrolling.
- **(5) A fork memo**: desk quant, researcher, or consultant — the game each one is, and your choice, with eyes open, in writing.

The MIT MicroMasters in Finance is a real credential program — confirm current requirements, pricing, and credit-transfer terms with MIT, since program details change. Interview difficulty varies by firm and by year, and nothing here guarantees outcomes. Interstitium Labs confers no certificate and is not affiliated with MIT.

scriptLabs.title: The Application Funnel Tracker
scriptLabs.brief: Build the funnel tracker: applications in, conversion at each stage, bottleneck diagnosis. The feedback loop as code.
scriptLabs.starter:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
# TODO: print conversion rate between consecutive stages
# TODO: print overall applied->offer rate
# TODO: diagnose the bottleneck (lowest conversion stage)
scriptLabs.solution:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
convs = {}
for i in range(len(stages)-1):
    r = counts[stages[i+1]]/counts[stages[i]]
    convs[f'{stages[i]}->{stages[i+1]}'] = r
    print(f'{stages[i]} -> {stages[i+1]}: {r:.1%}')
print(f'overall: {counts["offer"]/counts["applied"]:.1%}')
bottleneck = min(convs, key=convs.get)
print(f'bottleneck: {bottleneck} ({convs[bottleneck]:.1%})')
print('low response->resume/portfolio; low conversion->interviews; low offers->the close')
# Lesson: the funnel diagnoses itself — fix the bottleneck stage, not everything.

scriptLabs.title: Unit Economics Calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Model a venture's unit economics: CAC, LTV, payback, contribution margin. Verdict: scale, fix, or kill.
scriptLabs.starter:
cac = 120          # customer acquisition cost
arpu_mo = 25       # monthly revenue per user
margin = 0.8       # gross margin
churn_mo = 0.05    # monthly churn
# TODO: LTV, LTV:CAC, payback months, verdict
scriptLabs.hint: LTV = arpu*margin/churn. payback = cac/(arpu*margin). Bar: ratio>=3, payback<12.
scriptLabs.solution:
cac = 120
arpu_mo = 25
margin = 0.8
churn_mo = 0.05
ltv = arpu_mo*margin/churn_mo
ratio = ltv/cac
payback = cac/(arpu_mo*margin)
print(f'LTV=${ltv:.0f}  LTV:CAC={ratio:.1f}  payback={payback:.1f} mo')
if ratio >= 3 and payback < 12:
    print('verdict: SCALE — economics work')
elif ratio >= 2:
    print('verdict: FIX — improve retention or monetization before scale')
else:
    print('verdict: KILL or rebuild — scaling multiplies the loss')
# Lesson: unit economics before scale — the spreadsheet is the strategy.

scriptLabs.title: The Offer Evaluator
scriptLabs.brief: Score competing offers on total comp, growth, team, and your walk-away number. Decide like an adult, not from desperation.
scriptLabs.starter:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
# TODO: total comp per offer; score = total/walk_away weighted with growth, team
# TODO: print ranked recommendation
scriptLabs.solution:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
ranked = []
for o in offers:
    total = o['base']+o['bonus']+o['equity_yr']
    score = 0.6*(total/walk_away_total) + 0.2*(o['growth']/10) + 0.2*(o['team']/10)
    ranked.append((score, o['name'], total))
    print(f"{o['name']}: total=${total:,} score={score:.2f} {'BELOW WALK-AWAY' if total < walk_away_total else ''}")
for score, name, total in sorted(ranked, reverse=True):
    print(f'rank: {name} ({score:.2f})')
# Lesson: the walk-away number, decided in advance, prevents the worst mistake.

scenarios.title: The Discovery Call
scenarios.context: Prospect: 'We need an AI chatbot for support.' Budget approved. Timeline aggressive.

options.why: Building the stated solution skips discovery — the expensive mistake.

options.text: Discover: ticket volumes, resolution rates, what 'support' costs today, what happens if nothing changes
options.why: Diagnose before prescribing — the real problem might be documentation, triage, or staffing, not a chatbot.

steps.prompt: Discovery finds 70% of tickets are password resets. Now?

options.why: The budget was for a solution; the problem is password resets — self-service reset beats a chatbot.

options.text: Reframe: propose the smallest decisive fix (self-service reset) and prove it on a pilot
options.why: FDE value: solve the real problem, prove it fast — trust compounds from honesty.

scenarios.title: Two Offers
scenarios.context: Offer A: $95k + growth. Offer B: $115k, on-call heavy, stagnant stack. Walk-away: $100k total.

options.why: Total comp isn't total value — on-call and stagnation have prices too.

options.text: Score both against walk-away + growth + team; negotiate B's terms or take A deliberately
options.why: The rubric decides, not the salary line — growth and sustainability compound.

steps.prompt: B won't budge on on-call. A counters to $102k. Move?

options.text: Take A — clears walk-away, better growth, decided by rubric not impulse
options.why: The pre-committed framework prevents desperation decisions — this is what it was for.

options.text: Hold out for a third offer
options.why: Bird-in-hand with a good rubric beats indefinite holding — decide and commit.

blocks.body: Discover → Model → Prove → Integrate → Operate → Generalize. Diagnose before prescribing.
applied→response→screen→onsite→offer. Fix the bottleneck stage, not everything.
Technical: depth + speed. Design: requirements first. Behavioral: STAR + numbers. Offers: walk-away pre-committed.
E/I S/N T/F J/P — preferences, not destiny. Energy economics for fit.
Pain + budget. MVP = riskiest-assumption test. LTV:CAC≥3, payback<12. Default alive.
SAFE: cap/discount. Dilution math. Raise from strength or don't raise.
Proof-level math → probability depth → Python/C++ → internships → MicroMasters → fork.
d(W²)=2WdW+dt. The chain rule for stochastic processes.

answerBank.a: FDE is a deployment model: you ship inside customer constraints and transfer operations. It suits people who like diagnosis, customers, and ambiguity. Pure SWE suits deep-system builders. The arc's skills transfer both ways.
Three excellent beats ten mediocre. Each with a README (problem, approach, results, proof link). Quality is the filter hiring managers actually apply.
It's a preference instrument, not a medical device — useful for working-style insight, not destiny. Use it for energy economics and team design; never for hiring decisions about others.
Default: job first, venture as the side project until unit economics or traction demand full time. Default alive applies to your life too — runway matters personally.
Desk quant roles hire at bachelor's/master's with proof-level math and C++/Python. Researcher roles skew PhD. The fork is real — audit honestly, then choose.

If you want the credential and the degree pathway: yes, with the transfer math done first. If you want only the knowledge: the preparation map (this module) plus the underlying math gets you most of the way.
